narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak read negatively - 'Blessed is the man who WALKS not in the counsel of the wicked': walking named only to be refused. Type (102) is volition: not a felt state but an act of the will, a conduct chosen. Source (103) is absent - the reading does not trace where this refusal springs from; it reports the declining, not its origin. Seat (104) is none: the operation is not organ-located; it is the whole man setting a boundary, not a faculty switching on. Bearer (105) is the blessed man (inferred, to_span 275344): the interior of the one Psalm 1 pronounces happy. Operation (106) is the core event - 'the first refusal: he does not even walk in step with the counsel of the wicked, declining the casual first association.' Target (107) is refusal-1 (inferred): what the walk aims at is the refusal itself, the first boundary drawn. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked, the declining stated flatly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream result is booked, and it is not framed as a forbidding but as the blessed man's own choice. Coupling (112) is 'walk-not' (inferred): the reading is welded to its own negation - this walk exists only as a walk-declined, the refusal being the whole of it. Discovery (114) names the placement: the mildest, most casual involvement, walking-alongside, is already refused; the interior sets its first boundary. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the blessed man. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the refusal sits wholly inside, a set of the inner life. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the blessed man's will declines even to fall into step with wicked counsel - the gentlest first association refused, an inward boundary drawn before any deed, held as a settled trait of the inner life.
narratives.story: The very first line of the Psalter draws a picture of a happy man, and it starts not with what he does but with what he refuses to do: he will not so much as fall into step with the counsel of the wicked. This is a choice of the will, the mildest possible involvement declined at the door. Walking alongside is the easiest, most casual kind of company, and it is exactly this that he turns down - the first boundary of the inner life, drawn before any wrong is ever committed. The passage does not say where the refusal comes from or measure how firm it is; it simply reports the declining as the man's own settled character, a boundary kept quietly inside him.
narratives.variation_note: First of eighteen distinct walk-readings and the opening one in a three-step descent Psalm 1 refuses - walk (v1a), stand (v1b), sit (v1c). This reading is the mildest rung: casual walking-alongside declined. It differs from every later walk-reading in being purely negative and purely a boundary - no God-ward target yet, only refusal-1; the positive, God-oriented walks come later in the family.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is amad read negatively - 'nor STANDS in the way of sinners': standing named to be refused. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, a posture chosen. Source (103) is absent - the reading does not trace the refusal's origin. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole man takes, or declines, a position. Bearer (105) is the blessed man (inferred, to_span 275348). Operation (106) is 'the second, deeper refusal: he does not stop and stand in the way of sinners, declining to settle among them.' Target (107) is refusal-2 (inferred): the aim is the second boundary. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent - no degree, no narrowing, no booked result, and it reads as the man's own declining, not a decree. Coupling (112) is 'stand-not' (inferred): welded to its own negation, a stance-declined. Discovery (114) marks the escalation: standing is more settled than walking; the refusal deepens from passing-by to taking-a-position. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the refusal held within. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the blessed man's will declines to halt and take up a position among sinners - the boundary of v1a deepened, passing-by hardening into a refusal to settle, an inward stance held as a trait of the inner life.
narratives.story: The happy man's refusals in Psalm 1 come in stages, and this is the second, sterner one. It is one thing to decline to walk alongside the wicked; it is more to refuse to stop and stand where sinners stand - to take up a position among them, to settle in. That is what he will not do. Standing is more committed than walking past, and so the boundary of the inner life deepens here from merely declining company to refusing to plant one's feet in it. Again the passage gives no source and no measure; it simply shows a man whose settled character will not let him take his stand among wrongdoers.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'He who WALKS blamelessly and does what is right': walking as a whole upright manner of life. Type (102) is volition: conduct willed, not a passing feeling. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked behind the uprightness. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the life itself is upright, not one organ. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred, to_span 274617): the one who may dwell on God's holy hill. Operation (106) is 'the one who may dwell walks with integrity and does what is right - a whole manner of life without crookedness.' Target (107) is integrity-of-walk (inferred): the aim is a life of consistent uprightness. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'walk-blameless' (inferred): the walk welded to blamelessness, the two inseparable. Discovery (114): the operation is a consistent uprightness of conduct; the life itself is the first qualification to dwell with God. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the integrity held within, though it shows in conduct. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the one who would dwell with God walks blamelessly and does right - a whole undivided manner of life, integrity and walk welded together, held as an inner condition that qualifies the person for God's presence.
narratives.story: Psalm 15 asks who may live in God's presence, and the answer begins with how a person walks through ordinary life: blamelessly, doing what is right. Here walking is not one act but the whole shape of a life - a way of living with no crookedness in it. This consistent uprightness is the very first qualification for dwelling with God; the life itself is the credential. The passage does not explain where such integrity comes from or grade how much of it is needed; it simply binds the walk and the blamelessness together as one thing and holds it up as an inner condition that fits a person to stand on God's holy hill.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings; here the accent is on walking as the qualification to dwell with God - integrity of the whole life. It differs from Psalm 1's refusals (negative boundaries) by being wholly positive: not what the walker avoids but the undivided uprightness he embodies. The target has moved from mere refusal to integrity-of-walk, though the locus is still internal.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is mot read negatively - 'My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not SLIPPED': slipping named as what did not happen. Type (102) is volition: a maintained fidelity of walk, held by the will. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked for the steadiness. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole person keeps its footing. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 306042). Operation (106) is 'the self's steps have held fast to God's paths; its feet have not slipped - sustained fidelity of walk.' Target (107) is steadfast-walk (inferred): the aim is the maintained course itself. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'feet-not-slipped' (inferred): welded to the non-slip, the steadiness defined by the fall that did not come. Discovery (114): a maintained course; the interior has kept its footing on God's tracks. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the steadfastness held within. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist reports feet that have held to God's paths and not slipped - a fidelity of walk measured precisely by the fall it avoided, a sustained inner steadiness held as a trait of the inner life and offered as the ground of his appeal.
narratives.story: In Psalm 17 the psalmist can say that his steps have held fast to God's paths and his feet have not slipped. Steadiness here is described by the fall that never came: he has kept his footing where he might have lost it. It is a fidelity of walk, a course held to over time rather than a single act, and it belongs to the inner life - a steadiness the man carries within and can point to as the honest ground of his prayer. The passage does not say what kept him from slipping or how close he came; it simply reports feet that stayed on the track, a walk that did not wander off God's paths.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is shamar - 'For I have KEPT the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God': keeping as sustained loyalty. Type (102) is volition: a loyalty willed and maintained. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked behind the fidelity. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole person keeps. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 274987). Operation (106) is 'the self has kept God's ways and not wickedly departed from him - sustained fidelity.' Target (107) is fidelity (inferred): the aim is the maintained loyalty itself. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree scored, nothing narrowing, no separate outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'keep-his-ways' (inferred): the keeping welded to God's ways as its object, inseparable. Discovery (114): a maintained loyalty; the clean hands of v20 rest on this kept course. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the fidelity held within. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist has kept God's ways and not departed - a sustained inner loyalty welded to those ways, held as a trait of the inner life and offered as the ground on which his rescue rests.
narratives.story: In Psalm 18 the delivered psalmist looks back and explains, as he sees it, why God reached down for him: he has kept the ways of the Lord and not turned wickedly away from his God. Keeping here is a steady loyalty held over time, the conduct on which his clean hands rest. It is bound tightly to God's ways - there is no keeping in the abstract, only a keeping-of-these-ways. And it lives in the inner life, a fidelity the man carries within. The passage does not measure it or say where it began; it simply reports a loyalty maintained, a course held to, offered as the honest ground of his deliverance.
narratives.variation_note: First of three kept-readings (shamar). Here the bearer is the psalmist himself, and the keeping is his own past-tense fidelity offered as the ground of his rescue - first-person, retrospective, self-attested. It differs from Psalm 99:7, where the keepers are the historic intercessors, and from Psalm 119:4, where keeping appears as the divine charge laid on all. Same act; the difference is who keeps and why it is named.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is radaph - 'Surely GOODNESS and MERCY shall FOLLOW me all the days of my life': following/pursuing, but reversed - good pursues the psalmist. Type (102) is affect: not a deed the self performs but a felt assurance, a settled confidence. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked behind the assurance. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole person is assured. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 275854). Operation (106) is 'the self is confident that goodness and mercy will pursue it all its days - assurance of being chased by good, not evil.' Target (107) is assurance (inferred): the aim is the confidence itself. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'goodness-follows' (inferred): the assurance welded to the pursuing good, the confidence being confidence-that-good-pursues. Discovery (114): the operation reverses the usual - instead of enemies pursuing, the interior trusts that God's good is on its trail. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the assurance held within. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist rests in the confidence that goodness and mercy will chase him down all his days - a felt assurance, welded to that pursuing good, that inverts the pursuit of enemies into a pursuit by grace, held as a settled state of the inner life.
narratives.story: At the close of the shepherd psalm the singer turns the ordinary picture of pursuit upside down. Usually it is enemies who chase a person; here it is goodness and mercy that follow him, and they will do so all the days of his life. What lives in him is not an action but a felt confidence - the settled assurance that whatever is on his trail is God's good, not harm. The two, the trust and the pursuing goodness, are inseparable: his confidence just is the confidence that grace is coming after him. The passage does not say how sure he is or where the assurance began; it simply shows an inner life at rest, certain of being hunted down by kindness rather than by evil.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have WALKED in my integrity': walking as a life of consistent uprightness, offered as evidence. Type (102) is volition: conduct willed and maintained. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole life is offered. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 276111). Operation (106) is 'the self appeals for vindication on the ground that it has walked in integrity - a whole life offered as evidence.' Target (107) is integrity-of-life (inferred): the aim is the consistent uprightness put forward as proof. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked result, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'walked-integrity' (inferred): the walk welded to integrity, inseparable. Discovery (114): the interior stakes its plea on a consistent, undivided manner of life. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the integrity held within, shown in conduct. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist submits his whole walk-in-integrity as the evidence on which he asks to be vindicated - an undivided manner of life, welded to integrity, held as an inner condition and produced in court as proof of his cause.
narratives.story: Psalm 26 opens like a plea in a courtroom: vindicate me, because I have walked in my integrity. The psalmist offers his whole way of life as the evidence for his defence - not a single good deed but a consistent, undivided uprightness that he has kept up over time. Walk and integrity are one thing here; there is no separating the conduct from the honesty behind it. And it belongs to the inner life, a character he carries within and now lays before God as proof. The passage does not grade how upright he is or say where the integrity came from; it simply shows a man staking his case on the record of how he has lived.
narratives.variation_note: Second of Psalm 26's three walk-readings and one of eighteen in the family. This one is past-tense and forensic: 'I HAVE walked' offered as evidence for vindication (v1). It differs from v11 (H1980:walk#4), which is future resolve ('I SHALL walk'), and from v3 (H1980:walk#5), which is God-oriented ('walk in your faithfulness'). Same term and bearer; the tense and function differ - claim, pledge, and orientation are three distinct movements.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'But as for me, I shall WALK in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me': walking as a forward pledge. Type (102) is volition: a commitment of the will. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole person resolves. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 276124). Operation (106) is 'turning from plea to resolve, the self declares it will walk in its integrity, asking to be redeemed and shown grace - a forward commitment.' Target (107) is forward-resolve (inferred): the aim is the commitment to keep the course. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'resolve-integrity' (inferred): the resolve welded to integrity as its content. Discovery (114): distinct from the past claim of v1, this is the future pledge, the interior committing to keep its course. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the resolve held within. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist turns from pleading to promising - he will walk in his integrity - binding his resolve to that integrity while asking for redemption and grace, a forward commitment of the inner life to hold its course.
narratives.story: By the end of Psalm 26 the tone shifts from defending the past to promising the future: as for me, I will walk in my integrity. Where the psalm opened by pointing to how he has lived, it now closes with a pledge to keep on living that way - and in the same breath he asks God to redeem him and be gracious. The resolve and the integrity are one; his commitment is precisely a commitment to stay upright. It is a movement of the inner life, a will setting itself forward. The passage does not measure the resolve or trace its source; it simply shows a man who, having offered his record, now binds himself to keep the same course ahead.
narratives.variation_note: The third of Psalm 26's walk-readings, distinct from v1 (H1980:walk#3) and v3 (H1980:walk#5). Where v1 is a past claim offered as evidence, this is future resolve - 'I SHALL walk' - the interior pledging to keep its course. The shift from retrospective proof to prospective commitment is the finding; the study holds the two apart though the psalm, term, and bearer are one.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I WALK in your faithfulness': walking governed by God's love kept in view. Type (102) is volition: conduct willed. Source (103) is absent as a booked row - yet the verse itself supplies the informal spring: God's steadfast love before the eyes. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 276147). Operation (106) is 'with God's steadfast love before its eyes, the self walks in his faithfulness - conduct shaped by keeping God in view.' Target (107) is God-oriented-walk (inferred): the aim is a walk shaped toward God's faithfulness. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'walk-faithfulness' (inferred): the walk welded to God's faithfulness, moving in it. Discovery (114): the operation keeps God's love in constant sight and lets it govern the walk. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - held within, though oriented Godward. The full process: from no separately-booked source but with God's love held before the eyes, the psalmist walks in God's faithfulness - conduct governed by keeping God in view, the walk welded to that faithfulness, an inner condition shaped outward toward God.
narratives.story: In the middle of Psalm 26 the psalmist tells us what steers his walk: God's steadfast love is always in front of his eyes, and so he walks in God's faithfulness. Here the conduct is shaped by what he keeps looking at - the love he never lets out of sight governs the way he lives. His walking and God's faithfulness move together; he lives inside it. Though this is an inner disposition, it is plainly turned outward toward God, drawn along by the love he keeps in view. The passage does not measure the walk or file a separate cause for it; it simply shows a man whose steady gaze on God's love quietly directs how he goes.
narratives.variation_note: The third distinct walk in Psalm 26 (with v1 and v11). This one differs by its explicit God-orientation: the walk is governed by God's steadfast love kept before the eyes and moves 'in your faithfulness' - conduct shaped by keeping God in view, not merely the psalmist's own integrity. Where v1 offers integrity as evidence and v11 pledges it forward, v3 names what governs the walk. The difference marks a shift from self-attested uprightness to God-directed conduct.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is alach - 'together they have BECOME CORRUPT': to go sour or rancid, like spoiled milk, read of the whole of mankind. Read without valence-filtering, this is the family's descent-pole: not a walk kept but a nature turned. Type (102) is status: a condition, not a single deed - the state of being corrupted. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked for the souring; it is reported as an accomplished state. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole is tainted, not one organ. Bearer (105) is all mankind (inferred, to_span 279908): the universal 'they' of the psalm's verdict. Operation (106) is 'become corrupt / go sour' (inferred): the event is the turning-rancid itself. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object the corruption is aimed at - it is a state the bearers are in, not directed at anything. Manner (108) is 'together, as one' (inferred): the how is corporate - all souring at once, none by a separate path. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree scored, nothing narrowing, no separate outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) 'restates the corruption of v1 (shachat)' (span, from_span 279908 to_span 279886): this alach is welded to the earlier shachat - the same corruption named twice, first of the fool then of all. Discovery (114): the whole turned rancid; the moral corruption of v1 now spread to all together - a corporate rottenness, none exempt. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the corruption a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no named source and no seat, all mankind together goes rancid - a corporate corruption with no target and no measure, welded to the fool's corruption of v1 and now made universal, an inner state of the whole, none exempt.
narratives.story: Psalm 53 pronounces a bleak verdict over the whole human race: together they have become corrupt. The word pictures something gone sour, like milk left to spoil - a nature turned bad, not a single wrong act. It is a condition people are in, not something aimed at a victim, and it is not one person's failing but a rottenness shared by all at once, none of them exempt. The psalm had already said this of the fool at the start; now it spreads the same corruption across everyone. The passage does not explain what caused the souring or grade how far it has gone; it simply reports the whole of mankind gone rancid inside. This is the dark opposite of every kept and blameless walk in the family - not a course held but a nature spoiled.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is rud - 'I am RESTLESS in my complaint': to roam or be restless, the churning that cannot be still. Type (102) is status: a condition the psalmist is in, not a deed. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked for the unrest. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the whole self is agitated, not one organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 280122). Operation (106) is 'be restless / wander in agitation' (inferred): the event is the inner roaming itself. Target (107) is none: the restlessness is aimed at nothing - it is a churning, not a movement toward an object. Manner (108) is 'in his complaint' (span, from_span 280122 to_span 280124): the how is that the unrest is voiced as lament, working itself out in the complaint. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree scored, nothing narrowing, no separate outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired with moaning aloud' (span, to_span 280125): the restlessness welded to audible moaning, the two together the shape of his distress. Discovery (114): the agitated, wandering unrest of a tormented mind - the inability to be still, the churning that drives the lament, inner turmoil that cannot settle. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the turmoil held within. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist's inner life roams and will not settle - a targetless churning voiced as complaint and welded to his moaning, an unsettled state of the inner being under torment.
narratives.story: In Psalm 55 the psalmist describes a mind that will not hold still: I am restless in my complaint, he says, and he moans aloud. The word is one of roaming and churning - an inner agitation that cannot come to rest. It is not aimed at anything; it is simply the state of a tormented mind turning over and over, and it spills out of him as lament and moaning, the two of them together the shape of his distress. The passage does not say what set the churning going or how bad it is; it simply shows an inner life that cannot settle, wandering in its own unrest while the trouble presses on it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is shalach - 'My companion STRETCHED OUT his hand against those at peace with him': the reaching-out of a hand in violence. Read at full weight, this is the family's word for a movement turned to betrayal. Type (102) is action: a deed, the hand extended to strike. Source (103) is absent - no interior origin booked for the aggression. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the person acts, not an organ. Bearer (105) is the betrayer (inferred, to_span 280126): the trusted companion of the psalm, read from within his treachery. Operation (106) is 'stretch out the hand (in violence)': the event is the raised, striking hand. Target (107) is 'against those at peace with him' (span, from_span 280126 to_span 280128): the deed is aimed squarely at his own allies, those who held peace with him. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree scored, nothing narrowing, no separate outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired with violating his covenant' (span, to_span 280130): the stretched hand welded to covenant-breaking - the violence and the betrayal of a bond are one act. Discovery (114): the raised hand of the traitor, aggression against one's own allies - betrayal turned to open violence, the hand that had shared bread now lifted to strike. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:person - and this is the finding: the operation is directed outward at another person, not held as an inner state. The full process: from no booked interior source and no seat, the trusted companion extends his hand in violence against those at peace with him, welding the blow to the breaking of his covenant - a betrayal that moves outward onto another person, the family's reaching turned to open aggression against a friend.
narratives.story: Psalm 55 gives us the wound of betrayal from the inside. The attacker is no stranger but the psalmist's own companion, and what he does is reach out his hand against the very people who were at peace with him. This is not inner turmoil but an outward act - a hand raised to strike, aimed straight at his own allies. And it comes bound together with the breaking of a bond: the violence and the covenant-breaking are the same deed, the hand that once shared bread now lifted to harm. The passage does not say what drove him or how hard the blow fell; it simply reports a trusted friend turning his reach into aggression against those who trusted him.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'that I may WALK before God in the light of life': walking as a life lived in God's presence. Type (102) is action: a doing, the daily conduct of a life. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 280259). Operation (106) is 'walk / live': the event is the living-before-God itself. Target (107) is 'before God, in the light of life' (inferred): the aim is communion, life lived in God's sight. Manner (108) is 'in the light of life' (inferred): the how is that the walk goes on bathed in life's light, rescued from death. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'the purpose of the soul's deliverance' (span, from_span 280259 to_span 280251): the walk welded to the rescue as its goal - the soul is delivered precisely so it may walk before God. Discovery (114): the goal of deliverance, a life lived in God's presence - rescue from death issuing in communion, the psalm's radiant close. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the walk oriented outward, its reference-point God himself. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the delivered psalmist walks before God in the light of life - conduct that is the very purpose of his rescue, welded to that deliverance, bathed in life's light, and oriented wholly toward God as the one before whom he lives.
narratives.story: Psalm 56 ends in light. The psalmist has been rescued from death, and he names the reason for the rescue: so that he may walk before God in the light of life. Here walking is simply living - his everyday conduct carried on in God's presence. Deliverance and this walk belong together; he was saved precisely in order to live this way, out in the open before God with the light of life on him. It is a life turned outward, its whole bearing set toward God. The passage does not measure the walk or trace a separate source for it; it simply shows a man brought back from the edge of death and now living, day by day, in the sight of the God who saved him.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings. This one is the God-ward walk as the purpose of rescue - deliverance issuing in a life lived before God in the light of life, its locus external toward God. It differs from the integrity-walks of Psalms 15 and 26 (internal, self-attested) by making God himself the reference-point and the walk the fruit of being saved from death.

narratives.story: In Psalm 56 the psalmist speaks of his tossings - the restless, sleepless turning of a person in grief, the way sorrow keeps a body shifting on the bed at night. It is not something he does on purpose but a state he is in, the churn of anguish with no object, simply the unrest of a heavy heart. What is striking is that he pictures God counting each of these turns, storing his tears in a bottle - his hidden nighttime misery watched over and numbered by God. The passage does not say what caused the grief or how deep it runs; it simply shows a man whose sorrow will not let him rest, and a God who keeps tender count of every restless turn.

narratives.story: Psalm 58 looks unflinchingly at the wicked and traces their wrongness all the way back to birth: they are estranged from the womb. The word is one of standing apart, being a stranger - here, a stranger to God and to what is right, turned aside from the very beginning. It is not a wrong they fall into later but a condition they are born in, an alienation as old as they are. And it comes paired with going astray from birth: estrangement and erring are twins in them from the cradle. The passage does not explain the cause or measure the depth; it simply reports a wickedness that was never learned but was there from the start, a life foreign to goodness before it ever chose.

narratives.story: Alongside its verdict of estrangement, Psalm 58 says the wicked go astray from birth, telling lies. Here the emphasis falls on the doing: they actively wander off the truth, and they do it from the very start. It is not aimed anywhere in particular - it is simply a veering away from what is right - but it shows itself at once in the way they speak, in lies that come almost from the cradle. Straying and estrangement are two sides of one condition in them, deed and state together. The passage does not say what causes it or how far it goes; it simply shows a wrongness that begins at birth and starts talking - a corruption that lies before it can barely speak.
narratives.variation_note: First of two goastray-readings (taah). Here the bearers are the wicked, and straying is an ACTION - a lifelong veering from truth that begins at birth and shows in lies. It differs from Psalm 95:10 (H8582:goastray#2), where the same term is a DISPOSITION of a whole generation who go astray in their heart because they do not know God's ways. Congenital erring of the individually wicked versus the collective heart-wandering of a people: bearer and type both shift, and the difference is the finding.

narratives.story: Psalm 68 pictures God's enemies as men who keep walking in their guilty ways - not a single wrong but a settled condition of guilt they persist in. What the passage traces is not where the guilt comes from inside them but where it ends: God shatters the hairy head of the one who goes on this way. The guilt runs on, obstinate and unbroken, until God's blow stops it. It is aimed at nothing and bound to nothing in particular; it is simply a state these men are in, a determined guilt they will not leave. The passage does not measure it or name a partner to it; it shows the wicked's stubborn persistence in sin meeting the point where God brings it to a violent end.

narratives.story: Psalm 76 calls on all the peoples around to bring their gifts to the God who is to be feared. Here the movement is outward and public: nations carrying tribute, presenting homage to an awesome God. It is an act of reverence, gifts brought in fear, and it comes bound together with the making and keeping of vows - the offering and the promise-kept are one gesture of respect. The whole thing is turned toward God as its object. The passage does not look into where the impulse begins inside them or measure the reverence; it simply shows surrounding peoples doing homage, carrying their gifts to the God they have learned to fear.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'that Israel would WALK in my ways': walking as the obedience God yearns for but does not receive. Type (102) is action: a doing, a manner of life. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, God longs for Israel to walk in his ways - a manner of life welded to the listening he desires, oriented toward his paths, but named as a yearning precisely because the people withhold it; the obedience is present in the text as the thing God wants and does not have.
narratives.story: Psalm 81 carries God's own longing sigh: if only Israel would walk in my ways. Here walking is the obedient manner of life God wishes his people would live - conduct that follows his paths, the proof that they had truly listened to him. But the striking thing is that it appears as a wish, not a fact: God yearns for this walk precisely because his people are not giving it. Their obedience shows up in the passage as the very thing that is missing, the life God wanted from them and did not receive. The passage does not measure the walk or trace its source; it simply lets us hear God grieving over a people who would not walk with him, longing for the obedience they withheld.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings, and distinctive for being named in the negative-by-longing: God WISHES Israel would walk in his ways, which implies they do not. Where most walk-readings report a walk actually kept or resolved, this one reports a walk withheld and grieved over. Its locus is external toward God, but the emphasis is on absence - obedience present as the thing God wants and lacks.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'No good thing does he withhold from those who WALK uprightly': walking as God-ward uprightness. Type (102) is action: a manner of life. narratives.story: Near the close of the pilgrim psalm, Psalm 84 promises that God withholds no good thing from those who walk uprightly. Here walking is a straight, honest way of life lived toward God - conduct and uprightness bound together as one thing. It is turned outward, set toward God himself, and it is exactly this kind of life that draws his generosity. The passage does not measure the walk or say where it begins; it simply names the upright walkers and the good God does not keep back from them, a plain picture of a life aimed at God and answered by his goodness.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings; here the accent is that the upright walk is what God rewards - he withholds no good thing from those who live this way. Its locus is external toward God. It differs from the yearned-for, withheld walk of Psalm 81 (which God lacks) by being a walk actually lived and answered with blessing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may WALK in your truth': walking as the requested fruit of God's teaching. Type (102) is action: a manner of life. The full process: from no booked source but implicitly out of God's teaching, the psalmist asks to walk in God's truth - a manner of life welded to the united heart he prays for, oriented toward God, sought as the very fruit of being taught, an outward-turned conduct requested rather than claimed.
narratives.story: In Psalm 86 the psalmist prays, teach me your way, so that I may walk in your truth. Here walking is the hoped-for result of being taught by God - a life lived inside God's truth. And it comes bound to another request made in the same breath: give me an undivided heart to fear your name. The truthful walk and the single, whole heart belong together; he cannot have the one without the other. Notice that this walk is asked for, not claimed - it is something he needs God to make possible. The passage does not measure it or file where it comes from; it simply shows a man praying to be taught so that his whole life might move in step with God's truth.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings; distinctive as a walk PRAYED FOR rather than claimed - the requested fruit of God's teaching, welded to the plea for an undivided heart. Its locus is external toward God's truth. It differs from the self-attested integrity-walks of Psalms 15 and 26 by being sought from God rather than offered as evidence, and from Psalm 81 (a walk God longs for) by being longed for from the human side.

The full process: from no named source and no seat, the blessed people walk in the light of God's face - a manner of life oriented wholly toward God and welded to the festal shout of those who know him, an outward-turned life carried on under his favour.
narratives.story: Psalm 89 calls a people blessed who walk in the light of God's face. Here walking is simply their way of life, carried on under God's favour as under a warm light. It is a life turned toward God, and it is bound up with joy - these are the people who know the festal shout, whose glad acclamation and whose daily walk belong together. To live this way is to live lit up by God's presence. The passage does not measure the walk or trace where it starts; it simply shows a blessed community moving through life in the glow of God's face, their walking and their rejoicing part of one happy whole.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings; here the bearer is a whole blessed people, and the walk is life lived in the light of God's face, welded to the festal shout of joy. It is oriented toward God. It differs from the individual walks (psalmist, David) by being communal and from the trouble-walk of Psalm 138 by being bathed in favour rather than passing through danger.

The full process: from no named source and no seat, David's children fail to walk in God's rules - a manner of life that misses its God-ward mark, welded to their forsaking of the law, the walk present in the text as the obedience they refuse, still measured against God even in its absence.
narratives.story: Psalm 89 imagines a day when David's descendants do not walk according to God's rules. Here the walk appears in the negative - a life that has gone off God's path, obedience refused. It is bound together with forsaking the law: turning aside and abandoning God's word are the same failure. Even in the failing, the walk is still measured against God - it is his rules the sons were meant to follow and do not. The passage does not measure the disobedience or explain its source; it simply names a generation who leave the path they were given, the obedience God expected showing up as the very thing they withhold.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings, and one of the few read as failure: David's children do NOT walk in God's rules, welded to forsaking the law. It differs from the kept and blameless walks by being a walk abandoned, and from Psalm 81 (a walk God merely longs for) by being a defined default within a covenant warning - disobedience with consequences named. The locus stays external to God, who remains the standard even in the breach.

Bearer (105) is 'that generation' (inferred, to_span 285455): the wilderness generation. Operation (106) is 'go astray': the event is the heart's wandering. Target (107) is 'in heart' (inferred): the straying is located in the inner disposition - it is the heart that wanders. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, internal:ib-state (inferred, to_span 285455): the straying registered as a condition of the inner life. Locus (116) is recorded as 'paired with not knowing God's ways' - the heart-straying welded to their ignorance of God's ways, the wandering and the not-knowing one condition. The full process: from no named source and no seat, a whole generation wanders in its heart - a settled inner bent, welded to their not knowing God's ways, the straying held as a condition of the inner life rather than a single act, God's own verdict on a people whose hearts habitually turned from him.
narratives.story: Psalm 95 recalls God's verdict on the wilderness generation: they are a people who go astray in their heart. Here straying is not a single wrong act but a settled bent of the inner life - hearts that habitually wander off. And it comes paired with a deeper failure: they do not know God's ways. The wandering and the not-knowing are one condition; because they never truly learned God's paths, their hearts kept drifting from them. The passage does not measure the straying or trace its start; it simply reports God's own sorrowful judgment on a people whose inner life was set to wander, hearts that turned from him again and again.
narratives.variation_note: Second of two goastray-readings (taah). Here the bearer is the wilderness generation and straying is a DISPOSITION of the heart, welded to not knowing God's ways - a collective inner bent held as an ib-state. It differs from Psalm 58:3 (H8582:goastray#1), where the same term is an ACTION of the individually wicked, a lifelong veering from birth that surfaces in lies. The shift from congenital deed of the wicked to the settled heart-wandering of a people is the finding.

Type (102) is action: a doing, the observing of God's word. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the intercessors (inferred, to_span 285846): Moses, Aaron, Samuel - those who called on God and were answered. Operation (106) is 'keep': the event is the observing itself. Target (107) is 'God's testimonies' (inferred): the aim is God's word kept. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, external:god (inferred, to_span 285846): the keeping bound outward to God's testimonies. Locus (116) is recorded as 'paired with calling upon God' - the keeping welded to their calling on him; those who kept his word were the same who called and were answered, obedience and prayer joined. Discovery (114): the obedience of God's servants, keeping joined to calling. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source and no seat, God's servants kept his testimonies and statute - an obedience turned outward toward God's word and welded to their calling on him, prayer and keeping one life, the mark of the intercessors God answered.
narratives.story: Psalm 99 remembers the great intercessors - Moses, Aaron, Samuel - and says of them that they kept God's testimonies and the statute he gave them. Here keeping is the plain obedience of God's servants, holding to his word. And it is joined to something else the psalm says of them: they called on God, and he answered. Their keeping and their praying were one life - the people who obeyed him were the people who could call on him. The passage does not measure the obedience or say where it came from; it simply names these servants and the word they kept, showing an obedience turned toward God and bound up with a life of prayer that God heard.
narratives.variation_note: Second of three kept-readings (shamar). Here the bearers are the historic intercessors (Moses, Aaron, Samuel), and keeping is joined to calling on God - obedience and answered prayer as one life. It differs from Psalm 18:21 (H8104:kept#1), where the psalmist attests his OWN past keeping as the ground of rescue, and from Psalm 119:4, where keeping is the divine charge. The bearer shifts from self to remembered saints, and the pairing with prayer is distinctive.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'I will WALK with integrity of heart within my house': walking as integrity practised at home. Type (102) is action: a manner of life. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, internal:ib-state (inferred, to_span 268819): the walk registered as a condition of the inner life. Locus (116) is recorded as 'paired with integrity of heart' - the walk welded to the undivided heart it expresses. Discovery (114): the resolve lived out, integrity not merely pondered but practised at home. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source and no seat, David resolves to walk with integrity of heart within his own house - a manner of life welded to the undivided heart it flows from, held as a condition of the inner being and tested precisely where it is hardest to fake, at home, integrity practised rather than merely professed.
narratives.story: Psalm 101 is a king's charter for how he means to live, and it turns quickly to the hardest place to be honest: at home. I will walk with integrity of heart within my house, David resolves. Here walking is integrity actually practised - not just admired or thought about but lived out where no audience is watching. The walk and the undivided heart behind it are one thing; the conduct simply shows what the heart already is. The passage does not measure the resolve or trace its source; it simply shows a man determined that his private life will match his public office, integrity carried right into his own household.
narratives.variation_note: First of Psalm 101's two walk-readings and one of eighteen in the family. This one is a private resolve - integrity walked within one's own house, welded to an undivided heart, locus internal. It differs from v6 (H1980:walk#13), where the blameless WALK qualifies a servant for public ministry to the king. Private integrity versus the public credential of a blameless walk: the difference in setting and function is the finding.

The full process: from no named source and no seat, the one who walks the blameless way is the one who may serve the king - a manner of life welded to blamelessness, held as an inner condition, here functioning as the qualification for public ministry: the walk is the credential.
narratives.story: Later in Psalm 101 the king says who may serve in his household: the one who walks in the blameless way will minister to him. Here the walk is a credential - a blameless manner of life that qualifies a person for service. The conduct and the blamelessness cannot be pulled apart; to walk this way just is to be blameless. Where the earlier line was about the king's own private integrity, this one is about the character required of those around him. The passage does not measure the walk or say where it comes from; it simply makes an upright life the entry requirement for standing in the king's service.
narratives.variation_note: Second of Psalm 101's two walk-readings. This one is the blameless walk as a public credential - the conduct that qualifies a servant to minister to the king. It differs from v2 (H1980:walk#12), David's private resolve to walk with integrity within his own house. The same king's psalm holds both the private practice and the public qualification, and the study keeps them apart: the difference in whose walk and to what end is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is taah - 'Some WANDERED in desert wastes, finding no way to a city': wandering as lostness. Target (107) is 'in desert wastes' (inferred): the wandering is set in trackless wilderness, going nowhere. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, internal:ib-state (inferred, to_span 270011): the lostness registered as an inner condition. Discovery (114): the lost, homeless in the wilderness, the first plight. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the wanderers roam lost in desert wastes with no city to reach - an aimless state welded to their fainting soul, the outer homelessness and the inner faintness a single condition, the first of the psalm's pictures of human distress from which God redeems.
narratives.story: Psalm 107 tells of people God rescued, and its first picture is of the lost: some wandered in desert wastes, unable to find a way to any city. Here wandering is not something chosen but a state of being lost - roaming through trackless country, going nowhere, no home in sight. And the outward lostness has an inward twin: their soul fainted within them. The homelessness outside and the faintness inside are one plight. The passage does not measure the wandering or say how they came to be lost; it simply shows people adrift in the wilderness, hungry and weary, their bodies and their spirits equally at the end of their strength - the first of the psalm's portraits of trouble from which God delivers.
narratives.variation_note: First of two wander-readings under this char_key (taah). Here the bearers are lost travellers and wandering is a STATE of homeless lostness in the desert, welded to the fainting soul - a plight the wanderers suffer. It differs from Psalm 107:40 (H8582:wander#2), where the SAME term describes princes MADE to wander by God as a judgment. Self-experienced lostness relieved by God versus wandering imposed by God on the mighty: the difference in who wanders and who causes it is the finding.

Type (102) is disposition: a settled bent, not a single act - the way of life of fools. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the fools (inferred, to_span 269898): those made fools by their transgression. Operation (106) is 'walk in sinful ways': the event is the persisting in transgression. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, internal:ib-state (inferred, to_span 269898): the sinful way registered as a condition of the inner life. Locus (116) is recorded as 'paired with their iniquities' - the sinful ways welded to their iniquities, the two together the ground of their affliction. Discovery (114): the transgressions that made them fools and brought affliction. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the fools walk in sinful ways against God - a settled rebellious bent, welded to their iniquities, held as a condition of the inner life, the transgression that both marks them as fools and brings the affliction from which they later cry to be saved.
narratives.story: The second picture in Psalm 107 is of fools brought low by their sinful ways - people whose transgression against God is exactly what made them fools. Here the sinful way is not a slip but a settled course of rebellion, aimed against God himself, and it is bound together with their iniquities as one guilty pattern of life. This is what brings the affliction the passage goes on to describe. The passage does not measure the sin or trace its origin; it simply shows people whose whole way of living was set against God, and whose trouble grew straight out of it - rebellion that is its own undoing, until they cry out and are healed.

Source (103) is absent as a booked row - though the verse names God as the one who makes them wander, no source-row is filed; the reading reports the state. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Target (107) is 'in trackless wastes' (inferred): the wandering is set where there is no path. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, internal:ib-state (inferred, to_span 270022): the imposed lostness registered as an inner condition. Locus (116) is recorded as 'paired with the contempt poured on them' - the wandering welded to the contempt God pours on princes (v40), reversal and humiliation one movement. Discovery (114): the princes brought low, the mighty made to wander like the lost. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no booked source but by God's own act and no seat, the princes are made to wander in trackless wastes - a state of lostness imposed as reversal, welded to the contempt poured on them, the mighty reduced to the same aimless roaming as the lost of v4, an inner condition of humiliation worked on them from above.
narratives.story: Later in Psalm 107, the same picture of wandering returns, but now it is turned against the powerful. God pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes. Here the wandering is not something they fell into but something done to them - the mighty brought low, reduced to the same aimless lostness that the poor travellers knew at the start of the psalm. The humiliation and the wandering are one act: God strips them of their standing and sets them adrift. The passage does not measure it or file a separate cause; it simply shows the great ones of the earth made to roam like the lost, their power turned to helplessness by the God who lifts up and casts down.
narratives.variation_note: Second of two wander-readings under this char_key (taah). Here the bearers are princes and wandering is a STATE inflicted BY God as reversal and humiliation, welded to the contempt poured on them. It differs from Psalm 107:4 (H8582:wander#1), where the same term is the self-suffered lostness of ordinary travellers whom God then rescues. Wandering relieved by God versus wandering imposed by God on the mighty - the same word runs in opposite directions, and the difference is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'I will WALK before the LORD in the land of the living': walking as the life of faith resumed after rescue from death. Type (102) is action: a manner of life. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 271017): the one delivered from death. Operation (106) is 'walk': the event is the resumed living-before-God. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) here carries the reading's orientation, external:god (inferred, to_span 271017): the walk bound outward to the LORD before whom it goes. Locus (116) is recorded as 'paired with the delivered soul' - the walk welded to the soul delivered from death (v8), the rescue and the resumed walk one movement. Discovery (114): the life of faith resumed, conduct lived out in God's presence. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the delivered psalmist takes up his walk before the LORD in the land of the living - a manner of life oriented toward God and welded to his rescued soul, the walk that death had interrupted now resumed in God's presence among the living.
narratives.story: Psalm 116 is the song of a man pulled back from the brink of death, and here he declares what he will do with the life he has been given: I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living. Walking here is simply living again - the ordinary life of faith taken up once more, now carried on in God's presence among the living rather than lost to the grave. The resumed walk and the rescued soul are one thing; because his life was delivered, his walk can go on. The passage does not measure the walk or trace its source; it simply shows a man restored to life and choosing to spend it in front of God, the walking that death had threatened to end now begun again.
narratives.variation_note: One of eighteen walk-readings; here the walk is the life of faith RESUMED after deliverance from death, welded to the rescued soul, oriented toward God among the living. It is close to Psalm 56:13 (walk before God as the purpose of rescue), but where that reading stresses the goal of deliverance, this one stresses the resumption of an interrupted life. Both are God-ward; the accent differs between purpose and return.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who WALK in the law of the LORD': walking as a life governed by God's word. Type (102) is action: a manner of life. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the blameless (inferred, to_span 271197): those the psalm pronounces blessed. Operation (106) is 'walk': the event is the law-governed conduct. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): the walk welded to the whole walk/keep/run/stray arc that Psalm 119 traces through its length - this opening walk is the keynote of that arc. Discovery (114): the blessed who walk in the law. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the walk oriented toward God's law. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the blameless walk in the law of the LORD - a manner of life governed wholly by God's word, oriented toward God, set as the opening keynote of Psalm 119's long meditation on walking, keeping, running, and straying, the blessed life defined by a word-shaped walk. This same reading recurs at v3, where the blessed 'do no wrong but WALK in his ways.'
narratives.story: Psalm 119 opens by calling blessed those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the Lord. Here walking is a whole life shaped by God's word - conduct governed by his law from start to finish. This opening line sets the keynote for the entire long psalm, which will circle again and again around walking, keeping, running, and straying; everything that follows unfolds from this picture of a life lived inside God's word. A few lines on, the same idea returns: the blessed do no wrong but walk in his ways. The passage does not measure the walk or trace where it begins; it simply holds up the happy life as one that moves, step by step, along the path God's word marks out.
narratives.variation_note: First and keynote walk-reading in Psalm 119 (of several across the psalm), recurring at v3. This one is the blessed, blameless, law-governed walk that opens the psalm and sets the arc for all its later movements - keeping (v4), not wandering (v10), walking in a wide place (v45), running (v32), and the various strayings. It differs from those later readings by being the programmatic keynote rather than a particular turn within the arc; its locus is external toward God's law.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is shagah read negatively - 'let me not WANDER from your commandments': wandering named as what the psalmist begs to avoid. Type (102) is disposition: a bent feared, prayed against. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 271205). Operation (106) is 'not wander': the event is the sought preservation from straying. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): the wandering-to-be-avoided is a wandering from God's commandments. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): this not-wander welded to Psalm 119's larger arc of walking, keeping, and straying - the negative pole the psalmist prays to stay clear of. Discovery (114): the plea to be kept from straying. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the wandering defined by reference to God's word. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist prays not to wander from God's commandments - a straying feared and begged against, defined against God's word, taking its place as the negative pole of Psalm 119's arc, the wandering the walker knows he could fall into and asks with his whole heart to be spared.
narratives.story: Within Psalm 119 the psalmist prays, with his whole heart he seeks God, and then asks: let me not wander from your commandments. Here wandering is the very thing he dreads and begs to be spared - a drifting away from God's word. It is a danger he feels in himself, which is why he prays against it: he knows he could stray, and he wants to be kept. This fear of wandering is the shadow side of all his talk of walking and keeping - the negative pole he is straining away from. The passage does not measure the danger or say what might cause it; it simply shows a man who longs to stay on God's path and asks God to hold him there, aware that straying is always possible.
narratives.variation_note: First of two wander-readings under this char_key (shagah). Here the bearer is the psalmist and wandering is NEGATED - a straying he prays against, the disposition he fears in himself. It differs from Psalm 119:21 (H7686:wander#2), where the SAME term is affirmed of the insolent, accursed ones who DO wander from God's commandments. The psalmist's self-directed plea not to stray versus the actual straying of the proud: same word, opposite polarity and bearer, and the difference is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is shamar - 'You have commanded your precepts to be KEPT diligently': keeping as the charge God lays down. Type (102) is action: a doing enjoined - the observing of God's precepts. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 271827): though the command is universal, the psalm voices it in the first person as the one under charge. Operation (106) is 'keep / observe': the event is the diligent keeping. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): the aim is God's precepts observed. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked - though the verse says 'diligently,' the row leaves manner unmarked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the whole KEEP-arc of the psalm' (inferred): this keeping welded to Psalm 119's sustained meditation on keeping God's word. Discovery (114): the charge to keep, the psalm's premise. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the keeping oriented toward God's precepts. The full process: from no named source and no seat, God has commanded his precepts to be kept diligently - keeping named here not as a claim or a memory but as the divine charge, the premise on which the whole psalm rests, oriented toward God's word and set at the head of its long meditation on obedience. The full process: the command lands on the inner being as the standing obligation from which all the psalm's later walking, keeping, and straying take their measure.
narratives.story: Early in Psalm 119 the psalmist states the ground rule of the whole psalm: God has commanded his precepts to be kept diligently. Here keeping is not something claimed or remembered but the charge itself - the obligation God has laid down. It stands as the premise for everything that follows; all the psalm's talk of walking and running and straying is measured against this basic command to keep God's word carefully. The passage does not grade the keeping or say where the strength for it comes from; it simply names the duty God has set, the standing obligation the psalmist takes up as the starting point of his long devotion to the law.
narratives.variation_note: Third of three kept-readings (shamar). Here keeping is the divine CHARGE - God's command that his precepts be kept diligently, the premise of Psalm 119. It differs from Psalm 18:21 (H8104:kept#1), the psalmist's own past keeping offered as the ground of rescue, and from Psalm 99:7, the remembered keeping of the intercessors joined to their prayer. Command, self-attestation, and historical example are three distinct framings of the one act; the difference is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is shagah - 'the insolent, accursed ones, who WANDER from your commandments': wandering, here of the proud. Read at full weight, this is straying as the mark of the accursed. Type (102) is disposition: a settled bent of the insolent, not a single lapse. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the insolent (inferred, to_span 271724): the proud, accursed ones. Operation (106) is 'wander': the event is the straying from God's commandments. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): the wandering is away from God's commandments. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): this wandering welded to Psalm 119's arc of walking and straying - here the negative pole embodied in the proud. Discovery (114): the proud who stray from the law. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the wandering defined against God's word. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the insolent wander from God's commandments - a settled straying that marks them as accursed, defined against God's word, the actual embodiment of the negative pole the psalmist elsewhere prays to avoid; where he begs not to wander, these proud ones do, and their wandering is the very thing that curses them.
narratives.story: Psalm 119 turns to the proud and names their defining fault: the insolent, the accursed, are those who wander from God's commandments. Here wandering is the settled bent of arrogant people - not a stumble but a way of life that drifts away from God's word. And it is exactly what puts them under a curse. Just a few lines earlier the psalmist had prayed that he himself would not wander; now he shows us the people who actually do, and their straying is their ruin. The passage does not measure it or trace its origin; it simply holds up the proud as the living picture of the very danger the faithful dread - a life that has wandered off God's path and been cursed for it.
narratives.variation_note: Second of two wander-readings under this char_key (shagah). Here the bearers are the insolent, accursed ones and wandering is AFFIRMED - the proud actually stray from God's commandments, and it curses them. It differs from Psalm 119:10 (H7686:wander#1), where the same term is NEGATED in the psalmist's plea not to wander. The psalmist's feared straying versus the proud's realised straying: same word, opposite polarity and bearer - the danger prayed against here embodied in the accursed.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is ruts - 'I will RUN in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!': running as eager, quickened obedience. Type (102) is action: a doing - swift movement along God's way. Source (103) is absent as a booked row - though the verse names the condition ('when you enlarge my heart'), no source-row is filed. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; even the 'heart' here is the whole inner person freed, not an organ switched on. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 302604). Operation (106) is 'run in the way': the event is the eager running itself. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): the aim is God's commandments, the way run in. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked - though 'run' itself implies eagerness, the row leaves manner blank. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree scored, nothing narrowing, no separate outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): this running welded to Psalm 119's arc of walking and keeping - running is the quickened, joyful extreme of that walk. Discovery (114): the eager running once the heart is freed. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the running oriented toward God's commandments. The full process: from no booked source but conditioned on God enlarging the heart, and no seat, the psalmist will run in the way of God's commandments - obedience quickened from a walk to a run, oriented toward God's word, welded to the psalm's larger walk-arc, the freed heart breaking into eager speed along the path it loves.
narratives.story: In Psalm 119 the psalmist looks past mere plodding obedience to something faster and gladder: I will run in the way of your commandments - when you enlarge my heart. Here obedience is quickened from a walk into a run, eager movement along God's path. But he names the condition: this only happens when God frees and widens his heart. A cramped heart trudges; an enlarged one runs. The running and all his talk of walking and keeping belong to one picture, with running as its most joyful extreme. The passage does not measure the pace or file a separate cause beyond the freed heart; it simply shows a man longing to move swiftly and gladly in God's way, once God has made his heart large enough to do it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is halak - 'I shall WALK in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts': walking as free movement in the room God's word gives. Type (102) is action: a manner of life. Source (103) is absent as a booked row - though the verse gives the ground ('for I have sought your precepts'), no source-row is filed. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 271856). Operation (106) is 'walk': the event is the walking-at-liberty. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): the aim is a walk grounded in God's precepts. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): this walk welded to Psalm 119's larger walk/keep/run arc - here the walk experienced as liberty. Discovery (114): walking freely in the wide place the word gives. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the walk oriented toward God's precepts. The full process: from no booked source but grounded in his seeking of God's precepts, and no seat, the psalmist walks in a wide place - obedience felt not as confinement but as liberty, a life given room precisely because it is bound to God's word, oriented toward God, taking its place in the psalm's arc as the walk that opens out into freedom.
narratives.story: Deep in Psalm 119 the psalmist makes a striking claim: I shall walk in a wide place, because I have sought your precepts. Here walking is freedom - not the cramped, careful step of someone hemmed in, but movement through open, spacious country. And the surprise is what gives him the room: it is precisely because he has bound himself to God's word that his life opens out. Obedience, far from shrinking his world, widens it. The passage does not measure the freedom or file a separate cause beyond his seeking of God's precepts; it simply shows a man who has found that living by God's word is not a narrow confinement but a wide, open place to walk in.
narratives.variation_note: One of Psalm 119's walk-readings and one of eighteen in the family. This one is distinctive for reading the walk as LIBERTY - walking in a wide, open place, and precisely because the psalmist has sought God's precepts. It differs from the keynote walk of v1 (blessed, law-governed) by stressing the spaciousness obedience brings, and from the trouble-walk of Psalm 138 by opening into freedom rather than passing through danger. Same term and psalm; the experienced quality of the walk is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is shagag - 'Before I was afflicted I WENT ASTRAY': going astray, here the straying of the untested. Type (102) is state: a condition the psalmist was in before affliction, not a deliberate deed. Source (103) is absent - no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 272000): looking back on his former straying. Operation (106) is 'go astray': the event is the earlier wandering. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): the straying was away from God's word, corrected back to it. Manner (108) is none: no mode marked. narratives.story: Psalm 119 contains a candid confession: before I was afflicted, I went astray. Here the psalmist looks back on his untroubled days and admits that, without hardship to steady him, he wandered off God's path. The striking thing is what set him right - not comfort but affliction. The suffering he would once have avoided is exactly what corrected his straying and brought him back to keep God's word. He does not blame anyone else; he owns the wandering as his own former state. The passage does not measure how far he strayed or explain how it started; it simply shows a man honest enough to say that ease let him drift and pain brought him home - the straying named as the condition his suffering cured.

narratives.story: In Psalm 119 the psalmist reports both a danger and his answer to it: the wicked have set a trap for me, but I do not stray from your precepts. Here not-straying is a steadfastness held under pressure - a refusal to wander off God's path even when others are working to make him fall. The snare is real, the temptation to leave the path is real, and still he keeps his footing. This is the bright counter to all the straying the psalm elsewhere laments: where the proud drift and are cursed, this man stands firm precisely where he is most likely to slip. The passage does not measure his steadfastness or trace its source; it simply shows a person keeping to God's word under attack, unmoved by the trap laid to unsettle him.

narratives.story: Psalm 119 records a hard word about those who wander: God spurns all who go astray from his statutes. Here straying is a settled turning-away from God's word, and the passage does not soften what it brings - God rejects those who do it. It is the dark counterpart to the psalmist's own longing to stay on the path: where he prays to keep God's word, these are the people who leave it, and their leaving meets God's refusal. The passage does not measure the straying or trace its cause; it simply states plainly that to wander from God's statutes is to be cast off by him - the wandering weighed here not as a small drift but as the thing God turns away from.

narratives.story: For all its long devotion to God's law, Psalm 119 ends not on a note of triumph but of confession: I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant. Here the psalmist owns his own wandering - not the straying of the proud or the wicked, but his own, pictured as a sheep that has drifted from the flock. And he does not claim he can find his own way back; he asks God to come looking for him. It is a humble, honest close to a psalm full of high resolve, admitting that even the one who loves God's word can wander and needs to be sought. The passage does not measure the straying or explain it; it simply shows a man confessing he is lost and trusting God to seek him out.

narratives.story: Psalm 125 names a quiet danger. If wicked rule presses down on God's people too long, the psalm says, even the righteous might stretch out their hands to do wrong. Here the reaching is a temptation, not yet a deed - the point at which drawn-out oppression could finally bend an upright person toward wrongdoing. It lives as an inner pressure on people who mean to stay good but are being worn down. That is exactly why the psalm trusts God not to let the wicked's rule rest on the land too long: to spare the righteous from being pushed past their breaking point. The passage does not measure the danger or say it actually happened; it simply shows the honest possibility that prolonged injustice can tempt even good people to reach for wrong, and God's mercy in cutting it short.
